column1: Git: fork remote convention — what should `origin` and `upstream` point to, and how do you fix a direct clone of someone else's repo?
column2:
origin = YOUR fork (push here); upstream = the source repo (pull here). After a direct clone (origin = their repo):

git remote rename origin upstream
git remote add origin git@github.com:ME/REPO.git

Sync your fork's main from upstream (ON main, not a feature branch — pull acts on the current branch):
git fetch upstream && git pull --ff-only upstream main && git push origin main

column1: Git: why does rewriting a commit (amend/rebase) need a force-push, and which force flag is safe?
column2:
A rewrite makes a NEW commit hash; the remote still has the old one, so plain push is rejected (non-fast-forward). Use:

git push --force-with-lease

The lease aborts if the remote moved since your last fetch (someone else pushed); plain --force clobbers unconditionally. Always prefer --force-with-lease.

column1: Git: amend a pushed commit vs add a new one — which, relative to PR review?
column2:
BEFORE review / no PR yet: amend + git push --force-with-lease (keeps one tidy commit).
AFTER review starts: ADD a new commit + plain git push. Rewriting history breaks an in-progress review and comment anchoring.
Only rewrite branches that are exclusively yours.

column1: Git: split the last (single) commit into two separate commits — the sequence?
column2:
git reset --soft HEAD~1     # undo commit, changes stay staged
git restore --staged .      # unstage -> changes in working tree
git add -p <file>           # stage only hunks for change #1
git commit -m "fix: ..."
git add -A
git commit -m "feat: ..."

Verify: git log --oneline -2 ; git show --stat HEAD~1. Reverse if pushed: git push --force-with-lease

column1: Git: `git add -p` prompt — what do y / n / s / e do?
column2: y = stage this hunk; n = skip it; s = SPLIT into smaller hunks (only if an unchanged line separates the changes); e = EDIT by hand (delete the +/- lines you don't want, keep the rest); q = quit. Lets you commit one logical change out of a file holding several.

column1: Git: cherry-pick a commit onto a fresh branch — command and the stacking caveat?
column2:
git switch -c fix/login-type main   # branch off main
git cherry-pick <hash>              # replay that commit here

Stacking: a commit that depends on an earlier one must branch off THAT branch, not bare main — else it conflicts with / duplicates the missing prerequisite.

column1: Git: what does `git rebase --onto <newbase> <cutoff> [branch]` do, and why not plain rebase?
column2:
Replays only commits AFTER <cutoff> onto <newbase>. Plain `git rebase <newbase>` uses the merge-base and replays every commit since the common ancestor — in a stacked branch that wrongly includes a commit already merged upstream, causing a collision.

Ex (feat stacked on fix; fix already merged):
git rebase --onto main fix/login-type feat/token-refresh

column1: Git: rename a branch locally and on the remote — commands and the PR gotcha?
column2:
git branch -m new-name              # rename current (-M forces over existing)
git push origin --delete old-name
git push -u origin new-name         # push new name + set tracking

Gotcha: renaming a branch with an OPEN PR closes that PR (GitHub ties the PR to the branch name). Rename before opening the PR.

column1: Docker Compose: what does `docker-compose.override.yaml` do, and does it need `-f`?
column2: No -f needed. Compose auto-reads docker-compose.yaml, then MERGES docker-compose.override.yaml on top. Use it for local-only tweaks so the tracked base file stays clean (gitignore the override). `docker compose up -d --build` picks it up automatically.

column1: Docker Compose: a service with both `build:` and `image:` — what happens?
column2: Compose builds from build: and TAGS the result with the image: name. So base `image: vendor/app:latest` + an override adding only `build: .` -> builds YOUR code but stamps it vendor/app:latest, shadowing the published image locally. Override the image: scalar too (e.g. app:local) so your build gets its own name.

column1: Poetry: `virtualenvs.in-project true` is set but `.venv` never appears and install says 'No dependencies to install or update' — why, and the two gotchas?
column2:
The config only applies when Poetry CREATES a venv; an existing cache venv gets reused. Force a rebuild:

poetry env remove --all
rm -rf .venv "$(poetry config virtualenvs.path)/<name>"
poetry install --with dev

BIGGER GOTCHA: if VIRTUAL_ENV is set in the shell, Poetry uses it and ignores in-project entirely — unset VIRTUAL_ENV first.
